verses.text: Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children.
Walk in love, even as Christ also loved you, and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.
But sexual immorality, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not even be mentioned among you, as becomes saints;
nor filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not appropriate; but rather giving of thanks.
Know this for sure, that no sexually immoral person, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, has any inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God.
Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things, the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience.
Therefore don’t be partakers with them.
For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth,
proving what is well pleasing to the Lord.
Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but rather even reprove them.
For the things which are done by them in secret, it is a shame even to speak of.
But all things, when they are reproved, are revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light.
Therefore he says, “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”
Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise;
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing, and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God, even the Father;
subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.
Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body.
But as the assembly is subject to Christ, so let the wives also be to their own husbands in everything.
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it;
that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word,
that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without defect.
Even so husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself.
For no man ever hated his own flesh; but nourishes and cherishes it, even as the Lord also does the assembly;
because we are members of his body, of his flesh and bones.
“For this cause a man will leave his father and mother, and will be joined to his wife. The two will become one flesh.”
This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and of the assembly.
Nevertheless each of you must also love his own wife even as himself; and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

footnotes.content: What a tender call—to imitate God as a beloved child imitates a parent who loves them. Not in pride or presumption, but in the safety of being held. When we see Jesus live and die for us, we start to recognize what love actually looks like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Christ's self-offering was called 'a sweet-smelling fragrance' to God—language borrowed from temple sacrifice. It tells us the Father accepts His gift fully. When we walk in love, we walk in the wake of that acceptance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sexual immorality and covetousness—they're paired here because both spring from the same root: treating things (or people) as ours to consume rather than gifts to cherish. The Lord guards our hearts by calling us to something higher.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Foolish talking and jesting—not humor, but words that wound or belittle. The antidote is gratitude, which rewires the tongue toward grace. I've watched thankfulness soften many a sharp word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He names what bars the door to the Kingdom: sexual immorality, uncleanness, covetousness that makes an idol of possession. These aren't arbitrary rules—they're warnings about what the heart must release to follow Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Empty words can persuade us that sin doesn't matter, that God's patience means God's indifference. But Paul names the truth: God's wrath *does* fall on disobedience. Mercy and justice aren't enemies; they're held together in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A simple command that cuts through the noise: don't partner with darkness. Not in anger—just a clean separation. The Lord is calling us toward light, and He means it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once darkness, now light—the change is complete and already true. Our job isn't to become light (Christ did that), but to walk *as* what we are. The freedom is in agreeing with what's already been made real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The 'fruit of the Spirit'—goodness, righteousness, truth—these grow from His life in us, not from our striving. Notice Paul doesn't say the fruit is *ours*; it's His fruit, born through us like fruit on a branch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To prove what pleases the Lord—not to guess or fear, but to test and find out by living it. Each choice teaches us. That's how a child learns their parent's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No fellowship with unfruitful deeds of darkness, but even more—reprove them. This isn't judgment; it's speaking truth to what lies. Light doesn't compromise with darkness; it exposes it and calls it what it is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some things are so shameful that even speaking of them is a kind of pollution. Paul's reticence here is itself the message: certain acts belong in silence and renunciation, not in casual mention.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When light touches hidden things, they're laid bare—not to shame us, but to heal us. Truth is like that. It can sting at first, but it's the only thing that truly cleanses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes an early hymn or prophecy here—'Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.' It echoes both Isaiah's call and the resurrection itself. The Christian life begins in that awakening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Watch carefully how you walk—not obsessively, but with intention. Life moves fast, and an unexamined step can take us far off course. Wisdom means paying attention to the ground beneath our feet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Redeeming the time because the days are evil—not in fear, but in urgency. We're buying back moments from wastefulness, investing them in what lasts. Evil days make good intention precious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't be foolish, but *understand* what the Lord's will is. Folly isn't stupidity—it's the refusal to ask, to listen, to know. Wisdom begins in that simple act: 'What does He want?'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't be filled with wine—which clouds the mind—but with the Spirit, who clears it. One deadens; the other awakens. The contrast is stark because the choice determines how we move through each day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs—these were the worship forms of the early church. Singing to one another builds up what's fragmented. In melody we find a kind of unity the tongue alone can't reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Giving thanks always concerning *all things*—not just the good, but even the hard. This isn't pretense; it's trust that the Father holds everything. Gratitude is the language of those who've learned He can be trusted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ—not hierarchy, but humility before Him together. When we're both afraid of the same Lord, we treat each other with the reverence that belongs to His image.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord—the phrase hangs on what comes next. The submission is modeled on relationship with Christ, and Christ's model is self-giving love. Read the rest before you judge the beginning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The husband is head as Christ is head of the assembly—but Christ's headship is shown in redemption, not domination. Paul uses the language of ancient authority structures but fills it with the logic of the Cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As the assembly is subject to Christ, so wives to husbands—the model is our glad submission to the One who loves us. If a husband demands what Christ demands (everything) without Christ's sacrifice, he's asking for a god-thing he isn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Husbands, love your wives even as Christ loved the assembly and gave himself up for it—here's the reversal that changes everything. His authority is not power-over but power-for. He dies so she lives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That He might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word—Christ makes His bride holy through a kind of baptism, a word spoken over her. We are remade, not judged.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but holy and without defect—Christ's goal isn't control but beauty. He cleans us so we can shine, not so we'll obey.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies—he who loves his wife loves himself. This isn't selfish; it's unity. You can't despise or neglect part of your own body. Love here is recognition of oneness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it—even as the Lord does for the assembly. Care and tenderness are woven into nature itself. A husband's love should be the most natural thing in the world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because we are members of His body, of His flesh and bones—a mystery of union, spoken so literally it takes your breath. We're not just in a relationship with Christ; we're part of Him in the most intimate way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes Genesis 2:24—'For this cause a man will leave his father and mother, and will be joined to his wife. The two will become one flesh.' He's saying marriage itself points to the mystery of Christ and the Church.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and of the assembly—Paul pulls back the curtain. He's used marriage as a lens, but the real subject is always Christ. We were made for union with Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each of you must love his own wife even as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband—the final word circles back: love and respect held together. When both are real, the marriage becomes a sign of Christ's faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
